rv.q: Even so, “Master Class” remains a diverting and at times juicily amusing vehicle for an actress capable of bottling a prima donna’s blunt-force charisma.

During the intermission, I found myself wondering how Daly and her excellent director, Stephen Wadsworth, would keep all this intellectual and emotional splendor aloft. Though they’d captured my heart with the first half, there was the worry that exhaustion or lack of imagination would cause the acting or the directing to topple ...
Daly brings something better to the character -- a sense of vulnerable humanity that makes her courage to survive all the more
This Master Class contains a kind of Pyrrhic victory, an intrepidly honest performance that reveals a smart, yet tangibly scant show.
This paradox is the magic trick at the center of Tyne Daly’s remarkable performance as Maria Callas in “Master Class,” Terrence McNally’s 1995 play about the twilight of that goddess of bel canto.
This may be a flawed and even dishonest play, but it is a highly entertaining one, and Tyne Daly richly deserves her standing ovation.
Daly is sometimes ragged, but always courageous.
Daly takes a role that is cold and transcendent, wearing the marble Callas face well despite being some 18 years older than Callas at the time of the action.

It’s only fair to add that Garrett Sorenson and Naomi O’Connell, as two of Callas’s victims,delivertheirrespectivearias with real passion, and that Stephen Wadsworthhasstagedthepiecewith elegant simplicity. But, in the end, this is a show about opera for those who hate opera.
Stripping La Divina of both mastery and class, McNally shrinks her with a vengeance.
Well, that is who she was, as we learn from a playwright who knows whereof he speaks and from Daly’s triumphant portrayal of her.
Even if the play is essentially a monologue mixed with some opera selections, it makes for a thrilling ride and is one of McNally's most compelling works.
Tyne Daly's Maria Callas is a force of nature, commanding the stage with the kind of theatrical authority that makes you forget you're watching a performance.
Tyne Daly has made it her own with a performance that's both commanding and deeply moving.
The portrait is complicated and charismatic.
McNally's well-crafted, quip-filled drama — which depicts Callas teaching at Juilliard, circa 1971 — is less a biography and more a love letter to La Divina.
Daly, a forceful, convincingly complex presence in the coaching scenes, seems uncertain and unfocussed in the reveries (where Stephen Wadsworth's scattershot staging doesn't help).
Daly delivers a commanding performance that is a master class all by itself.
Her ego rises above her generosity of spirit making her Callas an unforgettable monster.
Tyne Daly's performance in this sturdy mounting is certainly bound to be one of the highlights of the season.
But Zoe Caldwell, who played Callas in the original Broadway production, was wrong, and Tyne Daly, for all her talent and appealing modesty, seems largely correct.
